title: Why I Turned Down My First Shoe Sponsor
creator: Kenji Alvarez
description:
People keep asking why I don't skate for a shoe company. Here's the whole story, the money part included.

Filmed at the Westside DIY spot. Shout out to everybody who keeps that place alive with their own concrete.

Footage: @tomasfilms, @riri.vx

sentences.t: Alright, so this question comes up in literally every comment section.
Kenji, why don't you skate for a shoe brand?
And the short answer is, I did get an offer, and I said no.
The long answer is this video, so, grab a snack.
Okay, a little background first.
I started skating when I was nine, at the park behind my middle school, on a board I found in a dumpster.
By fifteen I was pretty much living at the skate shop downtown, sweeping the floor for free just so I could hang out there.
And when I was seventeen, the shop put me on their team.
That's how it works for most skaters, the first sponsor is usually your local shop.
Being sponsored by the shop meant I got a free board every month, a discount on shoes, and a t-shirt with their logo that I wore until it fell apart.
No money, just product, and honestly I felt like I'd made it.
Then, two years ago, after one of my parts blew up a little online, I got an email from Vanta Footwear.
They wanted me on their flow team, which is basically the step before you're officially sponsored, free shoes and a shot at a real contract.
And a few months later, they actually offered me the contract, with a monthly check and my name on the team page.
I want to be clear, it was a good offer, and a lot of my friends thought I was crazy.
So why did I turn it down?
Reason number one was the shoes themselves.
I'd been skating their shoes for months on the flow deal, and they just didn't work for how I skate.
The soles were super thick, and I lost all my board feel, I couldn't feel the concave under my feet at all.
And I didn't want to spend the next three years filming parts in shoes I was secretly cutting the insoles out of.
Reason number two was the contract.
It had a clause that said I had to post a certain number of times a month, with their product in frame.
And I just pictured myself filming a line, landing it, and then having to reshoot it because the logo wasn't facing the camera.
That's not skating anymore, that's a job I didn't sign up for.
Reason number three is kind of the big one.
My friends and I run this DIY spot, we build it ourselves, we pour the concrete ourselves, nobody owns it.
And I didn't want my whole skating life to suddenly be about one company.
I wanted to keep skating with the same people, in the same places, for the same reasons I started.
Do I regret it sometimes?
Yeah, honestly, when rent's due, I absolutely do.
I work at a warehouse four days a week, and skate the other three.
But I also film whatever I want, wear whatever I want, and nobody tells me which trick to post.
And if a brand ever comes along that actually fits how I skate, I'd think about it, I'm not against it on principle.
If you're a young skater and you get that email, here's my advice.
Read the whole contract, show it to somebody who isn't excited for you, and make sure you'd skate that stuff even if they weren't paying you.
Anyway, that's the story.
I've got a new part coming out next month, filmed entirely at the DIY, so keep an eye out for that.
Peace.
